strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of object removal: removing associated shadows and reflections while preserving unrelated background content.

OBER is potentially valuable: it combines 2,875 camera-captured pairs, 10,000 simulated training samples, separate object/effect masks, and multi-object cases. The 343-sample RORD-Val evaluation also provides some evidence beyond the authors’ own capture domain.

ObjectClear has a coherent design: object-conditioned cross-attention is supervised using effect masks, and the resulting attention is reused for localized output fusion. Qualitative examples show convincing removal of shadows, reflections, and selected occluded objects.

Reported gains are large and consistent across PSNR, background PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP distance. The component ablation, attention-map visualization, in-the-wild evaluation, and 30-participant user study provide several complementary forms of evidence.
The paper is generally clear and well illustrated, and it explicitly discusses failures involving overlapping or very extended shadows.
weaknesses: The central comparison confounds the proposed architecture with privileged training data: ObjectClear is fine-tuned on OBER, whereas the baselines appear to be used as released, without training or adaptation on the same data. No SDXL or competing architecture trained on OBER under the same budget is reported. Consequently, Table 1 does not establish how much of the advantage comes from OEA rather than the new dataset, input formulation, or training regime.

The evaluation emphasizes global fidelity and background preservation but lacks a ground-truth metric restricted to the object/effect region. Global PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP distance can be dominated by unchanged pixels, and AG fusion explicitly copies the input outside its predicted region; this makes the large jump from 28.00 to 32.98 PSNR partly intrinsic to the evaluation. ReMOVE changes only marginally relative to the strongest baseline. Foreground reconstruction metrics, mask precision/IoU, and removal success are needed to substantiate complete effect removal.

The simulated-data formulation is technically unclear and appears questionable. Equation 1 derives a channel-wise alpha as (Igt-Iin)/(Igt+epsilon), which can be negative for bright reflections and is not, in general, a valid opacity estimate because foreground color and alpha cannot both be recovered from a single composite/background pair. The definition of the associated RGBA color layer and handling of invalid or channel-dependent alpha values are not specified, undermining reproducibility and the claimed physical realism.

Dataset quality and independence are insufficiently documented. Effect masks are obtained by thresholding image differences, but the threshold, alignment method, illumination controls, cleanup procedure, and annotation-quality measurements are absent. The train/test split is not stated to separate scenes, objects, or capture sessions. Moreover, 50 reflection pairs use manually selected model outputs as pseudo ground truth, which weakens the characterization of OBER as uniformly camera-captured paired ground truth and introduces possible selection bias.

The method description omits consequential details: which cross-attention layers, heads, resolutions, and timesteps are supervised or aggregated; the mask-loss weight; normalization of attention maps; how the inference mask is obtained; and Gaussian-blur/fusion parameters. Reporting recall alone (0.97) without precision or IoU is especially weak because a diffuse or oversized attention map can attain high recall.

The ablation does not isolate all changes from SDXL-Inpainting, including use of the unmasked input, visual CLIP embeddings, and the attention module. It also combines simulated-data components, so the claimed benefit of multi-object synthesis is not quantitatively separated from additional data volume, background diversity, or reflection pseudo-pairs.

The user study lacks uncertainty estimates, significance testing, participant/order randomization details, and per-image analysis. OBER-Wild has no ground truth and is evaluated using only one reference-free metric, limiting evidence for broad real-world generalization. Runtime, parameter count, and memory overhead are also unreported.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of object removal: shadows and reflections often remain when only the object mask is edited.

OBER is potentially valuable: it contains 2,875 camera-captured pairs, 10,000 simulated training pairs, separate object/effect masks, and multi-object cases. The combination of paired capture and scalable simulation is a useful contribution.

ObjectClear is intuitively designed. Supervising cross-attention with effect masks and using the resulting map to restrict fusion are sensible ways to remove effects while preserving unrelated pixels.
The reported improvements are large and consistent across RORD-Val, OBER-Test, and OBER-Wild. Qualitative examples also cover shadows, reflections, occlusions, and rough user strokes.
Ablations separately add mask supervision, simulated data, and attention-guided fusion, showing incremental gains; the paper also acknowledges failures with overlapping or very large shadows.
weaknesses: The main comparison does not isolate the method from its proprietary training data. ObjectClear is fine-tuned on OBER, whereas the baselines appear to be used as released without equivalent fine-tuning. Consequently, Table 1 cannot establish whether the very large gains come from OBER, the architecture, or both. The ablation lacks the crucial comparison of alternative architectures trained on the same OBER data.

Evaluation metrics are dominated by unchanged background pixels. Attention-guided fusion copies most of the input directly and raises PSNR from 28.00 to 32.98 dB, making global PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP distance especially favorable by construction. The paper does not report reconstruction quality specifically inside the ground-truth object/effect region, effect-removal recall, residual-shadow measures, or mask precision/IoU. Reporting only 0.97 attention recall is insufficient because an oversized mask can obtain high recall.

The simulated-data formulation is technically unclear and apparently erroneous. Equation 1 defines the background as Mo intersect Me, although object and effect regions should normally be disjoint and the background should be the complement of their union. The RGB ratio (Igt-Iin)/(Igt+epsilon) is not generally a valid scalar alpha and may be negative or channel-dependent, while Ioe is never rigorously derived. This prevents reproduction of a central dataset contribution.

Core implementation details are missing: the weight of Lmask relative to the diffusion loss; which cross-attention layers, heads, timesteps, and visual tokens are aggregated; normalization or thresholding of the attention map; and Gaussian-blur/fusion parameters. The text says the first-layer map is used, while the framework figure refers to averaged maps at the last step.

Dataset reliability and split integrity are insufficiently documented. Difference-threshold masks can capture registration, exposure, or illumination changes, yet the threshold, alignment procedure, annotation verification, and mask-quality measurements are absent. The manuscript does not state whether train/test scenes, backgrounds, or foreground instances are disjoint. Fifty reflection targets are manually selected outputs of the authors' own model rather than captured ground truth, introducing selection bias that is not quantitatively assessed.

The baseline set omits several cited, highly relevant 2025 methods, including SmartEraser, Erase Diffusion, OmniEraser, OmniPaint, and UniReal. Several comparisons also give baselines object-effect masks but then evaluate their expected alteration of that entire supplied region as a disadvantage, which does not fully resolve fairness.

The attention mechanism has limited demonstrated originality: stacked text/visual conditioning and attention localization losses are adapted from prior work, while attention-guided fusion is essentially soft compositing. The potentially stronger dataset contribution is weakened by the undocumented construction details and absence of a stated release or licensing/provenance information for downloaded images.

The user study is not sufficiently rigorous to support preference rates above 84%: it compares only two baselines, presents two variants of one baseline alongside the authors' result, and gives no information about blinding, ordering, image assignment, statistical uncertainty, or inter-rater agreement. Overall, the work has worthwhile ideas and promising results, but the evaluation confound and reproducibility problems currently make the central superiority claims insufficiently supported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of object removal: removing associated shadows and reflections while preserving unrelated content. The formulation is useful and clearly distinguished from ordinary mask-based inpainting.

OBER is a potentially valuable contribution. It contains 2,875 camera-captured pairs, 10,000 simulated training pairs, separate object and object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, and multi-object cases; this combination is uncommon in existing datasets.

ObjectClear is conceptually simple and practical: object-conditioned cross-attention is supervised to localize effects, and the resulting attention supports inference-time fusion without requiring an effect mask from the user.

The empirical gains are large and consistent across OBER-Test and the independent RORD-Val benchmark. Using only object masks, ObjectClear substantially improves PSNR, background PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP distance, even relative to baselines supplied with object-effect masks.

The evaluation includes numerous recent baselines, two mask-input settings, component ablations, qualitative comparisons, an in-the-wild benchmark, a user study, and examples with coarse user strokes. The qualitative results convincingly demonstrate removal of shadows and reflections in several difficult cases.
The manuscript is well organized and visually clear, and it acknowledges meaningful failure modes involving overlapping or very large shadows.
weaknesses: The quantitative evidence does not cleanly separate successful effect removal from background preservation. The largest ablation gain comes from attention-guided fusion, which copies most pixels directly from the input; global PSNR, LPIPS, and CLIP distance—and especially PSNR-BG—strongly reward this operation. Effect-region or foreground-only metrics are needed to substantiate that the same component improves removal rather than primarily preserving unchanged pixels.

The simulated-data construction is technically unclear and appears inconsistent as written. Equation 1 defines the background using the complement of the object/effect intersection rather than their union, which would overlap the subsequent piecewise cases. Its channel-wise ratio can also produce negative or otherwise invalid alpha values for bright reflections, and the definition of the RGB foreground layer is missing. Clamping, channel reduction, and handling of reflections are not specified.

Several details needed for reproduction are absent: the weight used to combine the diffusion and mask losses; which attention layers, heads, and tokens are aggregated during training; attention normalization; Gaussian-blur parameters; and exactly which base-model modules are fine-tuned. The threshold used to derive effect masks from image differences is also unspecified.

The dataset protocol leaves possible leakage and generalization questions unresolved. The paper does not state whether camera-captured train/test splits are separated by scene, background, and object identity. It also adds 50 model-selected pseudo-ground-truth reflection pairs, but does not isolate their effect quantitatively or discuss possible self-training bias.

The user study reports very large preferences but provides limited methodology beyond participant and trial counts: there is no discussion of randomization, participant screening, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty, or significance. Its comparison layout also presents both mask variants of one baseline alongside ObjectClear, which may introduce correlated choices.

The architectural novelty is moderate: stacked visual conditioning, attention-map supervision, and mask-based output fusion are adaptations of established techniques. The dataset, task formulation, and demonstrated practical gains provide the stronger basis for acceptance.

OBER is a potentially valuable contribution: it combines 2,715 captured and 10,000 simulated training pairs with separate object and object-effect masks, includes shadows and reflections, and provides captured and in-the-wild test sets.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad. ObjectClear is compared with numerous recent methods on RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and an effect-free MULAN subset. It consistently improves most reported metrics, including PSNR from 29.06 to 33.04 over the strongest baseline on OBER-Test.

The ablations isolate ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS. In particular, the large PSNR-BG improvement from 28.80 to 35.50 after AGF supports the background-preservation claim, while comparisons using ground-truth blending for baselines help address the concern that gains arise solely from copying unedited pixels.

Qualitative examples cover shadows, reflections, transparent objects, multiple objects, rough strokes, and failure cases. The 30-participant study also provides perceptual evidence, with ObjectClear preferred over all four evaluated competitors.
weaknesses: The central simulated-data construction is not specified rigorously enough to assess or reproduce. Equation 1 appears problematic: its first condition, p in the intersection of the object and effect masks, is inconsistent with the subsequent object case and likely should denote pixels outside their union. The per-channel ratio (Igt-Iin)/(Igt+epsilon) can also be negative or exceed one for bright reflections, yet clipping, channel aggregation, foreground-color recovery, and handling of unstable denominators are not described.

Many implementation details needed for reproduction are absent: the object-effect difference threshold, registration procedure for captured pairs, mask-loss weight, selected attention layers/heads and aggregation, attention-map normalization or thresholding, Gaussian-blur parameters, MLP dimensions, and the precise latent update implementing SVDS. Dataset capture protocols, background-image sources/licenses, and scene-disjoint split construction are also unclear.

Most full-reference metrics are dominated by unchanged background pixels, and AGF explicitly copies much of the input. The paper reports no target/effect-region reconstruction metric, boundary metric, or precision/IoU for the predicted effect mask. Reporting only 0.97 recall for ATA is insufficient because an overly large attention mask could obtain high recall while damaging unrelated content.

The modified ReMOVE metric used for OBER-Wild is described only briefly and is neither formally defined nor validated against human judgments. Consequently, the claim of superior wild-image performance rests mainly on a custom metric and selected qualitative results; ObjectClear is also second to OmniPaint on that metric (0.8470 versus 0.8656).

The novelty of the model components is moderate: supervised cross-attention localization, input-output blending, and region-dependent noise injection are individually straightforward. The paper repeatedly claims that ATA 'decouples' foreground removal and background reconstruction, but provides no formal mechanism or targeted evidence establishing such decoupling.

The user study lacks details about image sampling, presentation randomization, ties, participant screening, and confidence intervals or significance tests. The acknowledged failure on overlapping effects is substantive for the proposed task, since the method can remove another object's shadow or retain the target object's shadow. Overall, however, the useful dataset, strong external-benchmark results, and consistent empirical gains outweigh these reservations, supporting a weak accept rather than an unqualified accept.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important limitation of object removal: associated shadows and reflections must be removed while unrelated background content remains unchanged.

ObjectClear combines supervised object-effect attention, attention-guided fusion, and spatially varying denoising in a coherent framework. The individual components are supported by a progressive ablation: ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS each improve the reported metrics, with AGF producing the largest gain.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild, OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and a filtered MULAN subset, with numerous recent baselines and both object-only and object-effect mask settings.

The reported gains are substantial on paired benchmarks, including 33.04 dB PSNR on OBER-Test versus 29.06 for the strongest baseline, and they generally transfer to external benchmarks. Qualitative examples and a user study support the practical improvement.

Table 7 is a useful control: even when baselines receive ground-truth object-effect masks for background blending, ObjectClear with its predicted mask remains better on RORD-Val. This reduces concern that the results arise solely from copying the input background.

OBER provides paired captured images, explicit object/effect annotations, extracted RGBA foregrounds, simulated multi-object cases, and two test sets. If released as stated, it would be a useful resource beyond the proposed model.
The paper is generally clear and includes failure cases involving interacting shadows rather than claiming universal success.
weaknesses: Important parts of the method are not specified sufficiently for reproduction. The paper does not define how attention is aggregated across visual tokens, heads, layers, and resolutions; how the attention map is normalized for fusion; the Gaussian-blur parameters; or the precise algorithm for spatially varying denoising and background reinjection.

The simulated-data formulation is technically ambiguous. Equation 1 appears to produce a channel-wise ratio rather than a scalar alpha, does not state clipping or handling of unstable/negative values, and gives an unclear condition for the intersection of object and effect masks. The definition of the RGBA foreground used in the subsequent compositing equation is also incomplete.

The principal OBER-Test result is on the authors' own small captured test split of 163 samples. The manuscript does not explain whether splitting occurs by scene, camera, or object identity, nor whether foregrounds from test captures can enter simulated training data. These omissions prevent ruling out correlated train-test content.

Dataset provenance and release details are inadequate for a dataset contribution: Internet background sources, licenses, deduplication, annotation-quality measurements, and train/test isolation procedures are not reported. The manuscript only promises a future release and contains placeholder links.

The modified reference-free ReMOVE metric used for OBER-Wild is introduced without validation against human judgments or a detailed mathematical definition. Since that set has no ground truth, its quantitative evidence is consequently weak; ObjectClear is also not best on this metric.

The evaluation reports single numbers for stochastic diffusion methods without seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The user study similarly omits presentation randomization, participant screening, per-image aggregation, and uncertainty estimates.

The ablations do not fully separate contributions. For example, there is no comparison using the same training data with a conventional segmentation or auxiliary mask-prediction head, and no controlled analysis of different attention layers or fusion masks. Thus the claim that ATA specifically 'decouples' foreground removal from background reconstruction is stronger than the evidence.

Much of the performance gain comes from attention-guided input-output fusion, which directly copies background pixels. This is practically sensible and Table 7 provides a helpful fairness check, but robustness to inaccurate attention masks is not quantified; the documented over-removal and under-removal failures show that this dependency can be consequential.

The core architectural novelty is moderate: it combines SDXL-Inpainting, CLIP-conditioned cross-attention supervision, mask-based blending, and spatial noise control. The dataset and empirical performance form a stronger contribution than the individual modeling ideas.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important but under-modeled problem: removing not only a selected object but also correlated shadows and reflections while preserving unrelated content.

OBER is a potentially valuable contribution. It combines 2,715 captured training pairs with 10,000 simulated pairs, supplies separate object and object-effect masks, includes multi-object cases, and adds captured and in-the-wild test sets.

The empirical results are broad and consistently favorable. ObjectClear leads most metrics on RORD-Val and OBER-Test, and also performs strongly on OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and the selected effect-free MULAN subset. The margins on OBER-Test are substantial, including 33.04 versus 29.06 PSNR and 0.0342 versus 0.0521 LPIPS for the strongest reported baseline.

The evaluation makes meaningful efforts toward fairness: baselines are tested with both object and object-effect masks, and an additional experiment gives baselines ground-truth object-effect masks for background blending. ObjectClear remains best in that controlled comparison.

The ablations isolate ATA, simulated data, AGF, and SVDS. They show that ATA and simulated data provide incremental gains, while attention-guided fusion substantially improves background fidelity. Qualitative examples, difference maps, a 30-participant preference study, efficiency results, and explicit failure cases complement the automatic metrics.

The method is practically attractive: it requires only an object mask at inference, handles rough strokes and multi-object inputs, and uses the lighter SDXL backbone rather than the roughly 12B-parameter backbones of some recent competitors.
weaknesses: The dataset-construction description is not technically complete. Equation 1 appears to derive a channel-wise alpha under an implicit dark-foreground assumption, but the paper does not explain how the RGBA foreground color is recovered, how invalid or channel-inconsistent alpha values are handled, or how this procedure can faithfully transfer colored and distorted reflections. The cases in the piecewise equation are also ambiguous because the relationship between the object and effect masks is not defined clearly.

The claimed precision of the object-effect annotations is insufficiently validated. Captured masks are obtained by thresholding pixel differences, yet the threshold, alignment procedure, post-processing, manual quality control, and annotation accuracy are not reported. Small camera or illumination changes could enter these masks as effects. Dataset sources, licenses, split independence, and checks for scene/object overlap or Internet-image duplication also need documentation.

Several implementation details required for reproduction are missing despite the long appendix: the CLIP variants and token construction, attention layers/heads and aggregation, mask-loss weighting, mask resizing and normalization, inference thresholding, Gaussian-blur parameters, exact fusion equation, and precise SVDS reinjection procedure. The dataset link and interactive-demo link are placeholders, and no code or checkpoint availability is established in the manuscript.

Evidence for the central localization claim is limited. The paper reports only attention-mask recall, reaching 0.97, without precision, IoU, threshold details, or uncertainty. High recall alone does not demonstrate accurate localization and is particularly insufficient for AGF, where false-positive attention can overwrite unrelated background.

Most of the main ablation gain comes from copying the input background through AGF: PSNR rises from 28.04 to 32.77, whereas ATA alone changes it from 27.29 to 27.56. Table 7 helps establish comparison fairness, but the paper consequently overstates ATA as a strong foreground/background decoupling mechanism; its independent benefit is modest under the reported metrics.

The statistical reporting is weak for a stochastic generative system. Results lack repeated runs, variability, or confidence intervals. The user study also omits randomization/blinding details, participant screening, per-image aggregation, and significance testing. OBER-Wild relies on a newly modified ReMOVE metric without validating its correlation with human judgments.

The main method components are individually incremental—supervised cross-attention, input-output blending, and spatially varying noise/reinjection. The stronger originality lies in their task-specific integration and the dataset rather than in a fundamentally new generative formulation. Overall, the supported practical contribution favors acceptance, but the dataset and implementation ambiguities keep the recommendation at weak accept rather than accept.
